Issued at 217 PM CDT Wed Sep 16 2026

Tonight - Thursday: Rainfall Potential Tonight

Broadly anticyclonic flow continues to move east, allowing for 
modest moisture return to the region, even as the frontal boundary 
remains shunted well to our south across Central Iowa. This will 
continue to build north through the afternoon hours, increasing 
pWats, especially along and north of I-90, where they currently sit 
at less than 1 inch. A shortwave impulse in the entrance region of a 
passing upper level jet streak will likely create a vorticity lobe 
and an area of mid-level frontogenesis across Central and South 
Central Minnesota this evening. As this interacts with increasing 
moisture building from the south, an area of light to moderate 
showers is expected to develop/move into the region after 03Z and 
into the overnight hours. This should mainly impact areas along and 
north of the I-90 corridor. Areas further south across portions of 
Northeast Iowa and Southwest Wisconsin may also see some shower and 
weak thunderstorm development along a residual outflow boundary from 
showers and storms that move through this afternoon and evening. The 
bulk of the activity is expected to remain to our south across East 
Central Iowa but depending on where this boundary sets up, far 
southern portions of our area could see some thunderstorms with this 
activity given the modest amount of elevated instability (~500 J/kg) 
still expected to be present. Rain looks to be over for most by 12Z 
tomorrow morning with dry conditions expected for much of the day on 
Thursday. With temperatures in the low to mid 70s, enjoy those dry 
conditions because they won't be lasting for much longer...

Friday - Saturday: Increasing Risk for Heavy Rainfall, Localized 
Flooding Possible 

A fairly substantial setup for widespread rainfall across the local 
area is in store beginning Friday as a shortwave trough pushes off 
of the Rockies and into the Great Plains. As this occurs, rapid 
surface cyclogenesis occurs in much of deterministic guidance with a 
deepening surface low pushing into the Upper Midwest. As this low 
approaches, it will be interacting with an already present quasi-
stationary boundary which will allow for a frontal Maddox type 
setup to occur with 850mb moisture transport overriding the 
front and sloping 600-800mb frontogenesis northwest of the 
surface low and just north of the quasi-stationary boundary. In 
the presence of this forcing, weak but notable instability in 
the GFS/NAM atop this frontogenetic layer will allow for some 
convection to develop in this forced regime. Consequently, model
guidance continues to hint at a few county wide corridor of 
heavy rainfall where this frontogenesis aloft is maximized north
of the quasi-stationary front. Currently, the main forecast 
uncertainty with this conceptual model is the exact position of 
the surface low as it tracks eastward and into the region. Given
there is a fairly pronounced high pressure center near the 
Hudson Bay that will aid in advecting some dry air into the 
northern periphery of this system, the northern extent of how 
far heavy rainfall will get remains in question. That being 
said, the bulk of clusters in the grand ensemble 
(GEFS/EC/Canadian ensemble) keep the axis of the heaviest rain 
within the local area, with a tendency for areas near and north 
of I-90 at this time with this system. 

While exact location for the heaviest rainfall amounts remains 
somewhat uncertain, confidence is increasing for heavy rainfall 
where the strongest forcing manifests. Probabilities within the 
grand ensemble (GEFS/EC/Canadian ensemble) are already very high (60-
80%) for rainfall amounts over 1" within this axis of heavy rain and 
modest probabilities for over 2" (50-70%). When looking at the 
RRFS which remains the only CAM guidance available at this 
point in the forecast cycle, this follows this sentiment with a 
broad swath of 1-3" of rain and pockets of localized amounts 
over 4", which is to be expected in a convective setup like 
this. These locally higher pockets are also illustrated in the 
EC Extreme Forecast Index which has a shift of tails of 1 across
the region suggesting some members have rainfall totals 
approaching the 99th percentile of model climatology. This is 
shown in some EC members which have amounts of 4-7"+ where the 
heaviest rain occurs. Consequently, where these higher amounts 
do fall, river rises into flood stage will be possible along 
with flash flooding where storms frequent the same locations. 

Overall, the main state of the forecast at this point is confidence 
is increasing for a corridor of heavy rainfall across the region 
where 1 to 3 inches of rainfall will be common with locally higher 
rainfall amounts of 4 inches or greater possible. This will likely 
result in some flooding concerns where this occurs with uncertainty
